strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Implement a projected-gradient continuation search over feasible sample vectors. At each continuation stage, minimize a smooth log-sum-exp approximation to the maximum of all finite-support correlation scores; decrease its smoothing temperature and retain the best vector according to the exact evaluator objective. This is materially different from an explicit epigraph nonlinear program: there is no epigraph variable, no one-inequality-per-lag SQP solve, and no solver-status-based selection. Instead, every search step is a gradient step followed by an exact joint projection onto the box-and-mass feasible set.

The bottleneck is a nonsmooth maximum of generally nonconvex bilinear lag expressions. The log-sum-exp gives a differentiable objective with a direct softmax-weighted gradient, while continuation moves from a smoother search toward the maximum. The feasible-set projection enforces both bounds and mass simultaneously at every iterate. A supplied construction is used as a start and, when valid, retained as a fallback. A small multiresolution search and seeded alternative starts are heuristics for exploring other basins.

The exact facts are that the discrete objective is the maximum over all finite-support lags, the log-sum-exp upper approximation converges to that maximum as its temperature decreases, the supplied gradient follows by the product rule, and the capped-simplex projection enforces both constraints. The objective remains nonconvex; smoothing does not make it convex. Continuation and restarts may find a better feasible construction but do not guarantee improvement, the target bound, or a global optimum. The program must always select using the exact objective and retain a feasible fallback.

2. Mathematical specification

For a runtime length n ≥ 1, use zero-based indices, spacing dx = 2/n, and h ∈ R^n. The feasible set is P_n = {h : 0 ≤ h_i ≤ 1 for every i, and Σ_i h_i = n/2}. Define each unscaled finite-support lag sum for d = −(n−1), …, n−1 by q_d(h) = Σ_i h_{i+d}(1−h_i), where the sum includes only indices for which both i and i+d belong to {0,…,n−1}. Explicitly, for d ≥ 0, q_d = Σ_{i=0}^{n−d−1} h_{i+d}(1−h_i); for d = −s < 0, q_{−s} = Σ_{j=0}^{n−s−1} h_j(1−h_{j+s}). These are the 2n−1 entries, in lag order, of np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full'). The shorter overlap at nonzero lags is part of the definition; there is no wrapping or circular correlation.

Set r_d(h) = dx·q_d(h). The exact objective is C(h) = max_d r_d(h), which is exactly max(np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full'))·(2/n). Minimize C over P_n. Do not replace it with an autocorrelation identity or omit either lag direction.

For temperature τ > 0, define the search surrogate Φ_τ(h) = τ log(Σ_d exp(r_d(h)/τ)). If R = max_d r_d and m = 2n−1, then R ≤ Φ_τ ≤ R + τ log(m), and Φ_τ tends to R as τ tends to zero. Its derivative is ∇Φ_τ = Σ_d p_d ∇r_d, where p_d = exp((r_d−R)/τ) / Σ_e exp((r_e−R)/τ). Compute this with a max shift for stability. The surrogate is only a search device; compare and return candidates using C.

The derivative of q_0 is ∂q_0/∂h_j = 1−2h_j. For d > 0, each valid term h_{i+d}(1−h_i) adds 1−h_i to the derivative at index i+d and adds −h_{i+d} at index i. For d = −s < 0, each term h_j(1−h_{j+s}) adds 1−h_{j+s} at j and adds −h_j at j+s. Sum these contributions for each lag, multiply by dx to obtain ∇r_d, and combine them with p_d. These formulas include both directions and all boundaries.

For projection, the Euclidean projection of y onto P_n has the form x_i = clip(y_i−λ, 0, 1), with λ chosen so Σ_i x_i = n/2. The sum is monotone nonincreasing in λ, so bisection plus a small residual correction computes the joint projection. This is not clipping followed by rescaling.

When transferring from a source length a to target length m, treat source entry j as constant on [2j/a, 2(j+1)/a). For target bin k, let L_kj be the length of intersection of the source and target bins. Set y_k = (m/2)Σ_j h_j L_kj. This is the target-bin average of the piecewise-constant source, preserves its represented integral, and remains in [0,1] before roundoff repair. Project the result jointly after transfer. Compare exact scores at each candidate’s own resolution; do not assume transfer preserves the discrete score.

3. Implementation procedure

3.1. Write one complete program using NumPy and, if useful, math. Define all helpers at module top level; do not use nested function definitions, closures, or lambdas. Implement the required top-level entry point run(seed=42, **kwargs). Ignore unrecognized kwargs. Use one seeded NumPy Generator for reproducible starts, falling back to seed 42 if constructing a generator from the supplied seed raises an exception. Do not use filesystem or network access, print output, or mutate the pre-imported initial_h_values global.

3.2. Implement exact_c5(h). Convert a candidate to a private float64 array, require a nonempty one-dimensional finite vector, compute c = np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full'), and return float(max(c)·(2.0/len(h))). This is the authoritative score; do not return a surrogate value or rely on an unspecified signature for the pre-imported evaluator. Implement a separate feasibility predicate requiring one-dimensional nonempty finite values, exact bounds 0 ≤ h_i ≤ 1, and absolute mass error |Σh−n/2| ≤ 1e−9. Only call exact_c5 for candidates that pass this predicate.

3.3. Implement project_box_mass(y) for a finite one-dimensional vector of length n. If its shape is unusable or any entry is nonfinite, return the length-n uniform vector 0.5 when n is known; callers must otherwise use their own valid uniform fallback. For finite inputs, cap extreme values to a safe range such as [−1e6, 1e6]. Set low = min(y)−1 and high = max(y); at low the clipped vector is all ones and at high it is all zeros. Perform 60 bisection iterations. At each midpoint λ, compute x = clip(y−λ, 0, 1); if Σx > n/2, raise low to λ, otherwise lower high to λ. Use the final midpoint to form x. Correct the residual n/2−Σx deterministically by scanning entries and adding no more than 1−x_i when it is positive, or subtracting no more than x_i when it is negative. Keep all updates within bounds. Recheck bounds and mass; if the check fails, return 0.5 at length n. This helper is the only repair mechanism for proposals and starts.

3.4. Read the optional parent with globals().get('initial_h_values', None), convert it to a private float64 copy inside a guarded conversion, and never assign to the global. Use it only if it is one-dimensional, nonempty, and finite. Record n0 = len(parent). Classify it as an originally feasible parent if its bounds are within 1e−10 of [0,1] and its mass error is at most 1e−8; regardless, pass a usable finite parent through project_box_mass before searching or storing it. If the originally feasible parent exists, store its projected copy and exact score as the protected fallback. If a finite one-dimensional parent exists but fails the original feasibility check, use a uniform vector of length n0 as the protected fallback and also retain the projected parent as a feasible search candidate. If no usable parent exists, use n0 = 45 and the length-45 uniform vector as fallback and starting base. The uniform fallback is always feasible.

Maintain a global best tuple (score, vector copy, length), initially the protected fallback and its recomputed exact score. Also evaluate the projected finite parent as a candidate when available. Update a stored best only when a feasible candidate’s exact score is lower by more than 1e−12; ties retain the existing vector. Keep the protected fallback separately so later failures cannot discard it.

3.5. Implement an area-transfer helper using bin overlaps without allocating a dense resampling matrix. For each target bin, find only source bins that overlap it, accumulate Σ_j h_j L_kj, and multiply by m/2. A two-pointer traversal over the source and target partitions is sufficient. Project the resulting target vector to correct floating-point residuals. Use this helper for every resolution change.

Set the optimization cap to 180 samples. If n0 ≤ 180, form the distinct increasing levels from n0, 2n0, and 4n0 after removing values greater than 180. If n0 > 180, use only the optimization level 180; keep and score the parent or its projected copy at its original length as a separate candidate/fallback. At the first level, use the projected parent or its area-transferred copy as the base if a finite parent exists; otherwise use uniform 0.5. At each later level, transfer the exact-score best vector from the preceding level and use it as the new base. Do not compare raw lag sums across sizes; compare normalized exact C scores.

3.6. Implement top-level helpers smooth_value(h, tau) and smooth_value_gradient(h, tau). Compute q with np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full') and r = q·(2/n). For stable log-sum-exp, let R = max(r), e = exp((r−R)/tau), Z = Σe; return Φ = R + tau·log(Z). For the gradient helper, also form p = e/Z and initialize a length-n zero gradient. Iterate d from −(n−1) through n−1, with lag-array index d+n−1. Multiply each p entry by dx. For d ≥ 0, let L=n−d: add dx·p_d·(1−h[0:L]) to gradient slice d:d+L and subtract dx·p_d·h[d:d+L] from slice 0:L. For d=−s < 0, let L=n−s: add dx·p_d·(1−h[s:s+L]) to slice 0:L and subtract dx·p_d·h[0:L] from slice s:s+L. At d=0 these two updates combine to 1−2h. Reject nonfinite values or gradients. Do not form a (2n−1)-by-n Jacobian or use finite differences.

3.7. Implement optimize_start(h0, temperatures, iteration_limit) as a top-level helper returning (best_path_vector, best_path_score, final_continuation_vector). Project h0, verify feasibility, and score it exactly; use it as both the local best and current iterate. Use the fixed decreasing temperatures in section 4. For each temperature, compute Φ and its gradient at the current iterate. Initialize alpha to max(0.5, n/45) and cap it at max(alpha, 8n/45). For at most 50 iterations at that temperature, try at most 16 projected-gradient line-search proposals. A proposal is y = project_box_mass(x−alpha·g), with d = y−x. If max(abs(d)) ≤ 1e−8, or the proposal is not feasible, stop that temperature’s inner loop. Let slope = dot(g,d); if it is not negative, halve alpha and try again. Otherwise compute Φ_tau(y) and accept y as the next search iterate only if Φ_tau(y) ≤ Φ_tau(x) + 1e−4·slope + 1e−12·max(1,|Φ_tau(x)|). On rejection halve alpha. If no proposal is accepted, end this temperature stage but continue to the next, lower temperature using the current feasible x.

After an accepted proposal, compute its exact C with exact_c5 and update the local best only by exact-score comparison. Set x to the accepted proposal and increase alpha to min(1.25·alpha, alpha_max). If the projected step is tiny, stop the stage. Also stop a stage after five consecutive accepted steps whose surrogate decrease is no more than 1e−12; otherwise reset that counter. Continue from the final x of each temperature stage. The helper returns the best exact-scoring feasible point visited, not necessarily the final continuation iterate. A failed or nonfinite gradient returns the best feasible point already stored. The line search chooses transient search iterates by the smooth surrogate; only exact-scored feasible points can become returned candidates.

3.8. Use temperatures [0.06, 0.02, 0.006, 0.002, 0.0007] in score units, with 50 iterations per temperature. At each resolution, score the base and initialize a level-best vector. Process at most five starts sequentially, updating the level and global best after each start and its optimization. If there is no finite parent and this is the first level, use these five starts: uniform; project(0.5+0.4 cos(2πi/n)); project(0.5+0.4 cos(4πi/n+0.7)); a seeded random balanced binary vector; and project(0.5+0.25 times seeded standard-normal noise). Construct the balanced binary vector by choosing a seeded permutation, assigning n//2 entries to 1, and, for odd n, assigning one other entry to 0.5; all remaining entries are 0.

If a finite parent is available, or at a later level, use the base first. Then, in sequence, make projected perturbations of the current level-best vector with independent standard-normal noise scales 0.05 and 0.20; because starts are processed sequentially, center each perturbation on the best exact-scoring vector found so far at that level. Use a seeded balanced binary start next. For the fifth start use project(0.5+0.4 cos(2πi/n+theta)+0.10·noise), with theta uniform on [0,2π) and seeded standard-normal noise. Project every start, check feasibility, and score it exactly before optimization. For each start, catch an exception or nonfinite result from the optimizer, retain that start, and continue. Update level-best and global-best only from feasible vectors and their exact scores. Use level-best as the source for the next resolution.

3.9. Before return, project a private copy of the stored global-best vector once more and verify its length, finiteness, strict bounds, and mass. Recompute its exact score. Recompute and compare the protected fallback score as well; return the lower exact-scoring feasible choice, retaining the existing choice on a tie. If the stored best fails final validation, use the protected fallback. If that is unusable, use a length-45 vector of 0.5. Return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with h_values a float64 NumPy array, c5_bound the freshly computed exact score, and n_points = int(len(h_values)).

4. Search choices and useful variations

Correctness requirements are fixed: finite-support full correlation over all 2n−1 lags; the exact normalization dx=2/n; joint projection onto both bounds and mass; exact-score comparison for every stored solution; and a valid fallback. The concrete default is a maximum optimized length of 180; levels n0, 2n0, 4n0 filtered to that cap; five starts per level; the five temperatures and 50 iterations per temperature specified above; 16 backtracking trials; Armijo coefficient 1e−4; alpha halving on rejection and 1.25 growth after acceptance; and seeded randomness. The alpha initialization and cap scale with n because the gradient of the normalized score contains dx. These defaults require no preliminary tuning.

A coder may use a cap between 128 and 256, 3–8 starts, 40–100 iterations per temperature, and 4–6 strictly decreasing positive temperatures. Practical initial temperatures are 0.03–0.10 and final temperatures 0.0005–0.003 in score units. Perturbation scales between 0.02 and 0.30 are reasonable search choices. Keep line-search and iteration limits finite, keep all proposals projected, and preserve exact-score acceptance and the fallback rule. Any resolution or search variation must still score candidates at their own lengths with the exact formula. These are heuristics, not evidence that a particular score will be reached.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

Use float64 throughout. The max-shifted softmax prevents exponential overflow; underflow of sufficiently small weights to zero is harmless because the maximum entry contributes one before normalization. Require tau > 0. Check the surrogate, gradient, and proposals for finiteness. Reject nonfinite optimizer values; cap extreme finite proposal inputs in the projection helper before bisection. The water-filling residual correction must keep entries inside [0,1], and a failed projection returns the uniform feasible vector.

The search is bounded by at most three resolutions, five starts per resolution, five temperatures, 50 outer iterations per temperature, and 16 line-search proposals per outer iteration. A failed line search ends only its current temperature stage; a failed start does not stop other starts. Always retain the best exact-scoring feasible candidate and the protected fallback. No convergence or solver-success claim is needed.

At the optimization cap n=180, the lag vector has length 359 and the gradient length 180. Gradient accumulation is performed using slices and one lag loop, so extra working memory is O(n), not O(n²) for a stored Jacobian and never O(n³). Correlation work is quadratic in n but its output is linear in n; at the specified cap it remains small. A supplied parent longer than the cap is scored and retained at its own length, while optimization uses its area transfer to length 180. Resampling should traverse overlapping bins without a dense matrix. Keep execution serial for the one-CPU environment.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

All input checks, parent handling, projection, starts, search loops, exact scoring, candidate feasibility checks, and fallback selection must execute inside the generated run function and its top-level helpers. A missing, malformed, empty, or nonfinite parent must lead to a feasible uniform fallback; a finite but infeasible parent may be projected for a search start but must not serve as the protected fallback. Do not overwrite initial_h_values. Catch failures per start so one invalid operation cannot discard previously stored feasible candidates.

Before storing any candidate, require a finite one-dimensional vector, exact bounds, and mass within 1e−9 of n/2. Compute its score as max(np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full'))·(2.0/n), including both lag directions and finite boundaries. Use that exact score—not Φ, a gradient norm, or a solver-like status—to select the result. Recheck and rescore the final returned vector in the program. If search or finalization fails, return the best already stored feasible vector; if none exists, return the validated parent copy, or the length-45 uniform vector when no usable parent exists. The only return value is the required three-tuple, with the score matching the returned vector and its returned length.
